stories.topic: Walking Into an Invisible Glass Wall
stories.summary: In a very well-maintained office, Ajay was mid-sentence when he took an abrupt right turn to fetch his computer from a room. He walked straight into a glass wall that had been wiped so clean nothing showed it was there, and hurt himself a little. Amit teased him about it, then used it as the episode's opening metaphor: the state is like an invisible fist that gets in your way when you least expect it. Ajay agreed that the state invisibly reshapes our lives and now and then slams into us.
stories.insight: We have normalised the state so completely that we stop seeing it until we collide with it. The episode's project is to make that invisible wall visible.
stories.quote: I abruptly took a right turn trying to go into the room to get my computer that was sitting there. And in fact I crashed into the glass wall and I got hurt a little.

stories.topic: The Poker Stable: Memorisers vs. Askers of Why
stories.summary: In Amit's years as a professional poker player, many pros started out in a 'stable'. A successful player who could only play so many hands himself would stake a group of players and coach them in mechanics: with twenty big blinds, here is your reshove range; in this spot, this is your equity against that range. Most players learned these by rote and played correctly. Only a small fraction of winning players, who were already a small fraction of all players, worked things out from first principles. Amit says he was always asking why.
stories.insight: Memorised mechanics let you play correctly in situations someone has already solved for you. Asking why gives you an understanding you can carry into any field. It is more cumbersome, but it is what separates the rare masters.
stories.quote: I would notice in a lot of cases, players are playing correctly because they've memorized what to do from the theory, but they're not thinking from first principles and figuring out shit themselves.

stories.topic: Where Your Taxes Go: Moustache Allowances and Sandstone Elephants
stories.summary: On his old blog India Uncut, Amit ran a series called 'Where Your Taxes Go' that passed number eighty and kept going. He read out examples of state spending: moustache allowances, educating and rehabilitating monkeys, overpaying for condoms, policing parrots, salaries for fake municipal employees who don't exist, golf buggies for the army, countless statues, sixty-two sandstone elephants, and the regulation of skirt hemlines.
stories.insight: Each of these comes out of money collected under coercion, and that cost falls even on the poorest. Seen that way, an absurd line item is a moral question as well as a waste.
stories.quote: sixty-two sandstone elephants is what I see on my list and regulating skirt hemlines, which is also sort of something that the state has done.

stories.topic: The Restaurant That Must Break the Law
stories.summary: In an early episode of The Seen and the Unseen, restaurateur Madhu Menon described the many licences a restaurant in Bangalore needed. The excise department, wanting to track alcohol coming in and going out, allowed only one door. The fire safety department required multiple doors. No restaurant could satisfy both rules, and restaurateurs across India end up paying thirty or forty bribes a month just to operate.
stories.insight: A state with too much scope produces rules that cannot all be obeyed. That turns every business into a lawbreaker by default and stops society from solving its own problems.
stories.quote: you're breaking the law no matter what the hell you do.

stories.topic: America Was Built by Mad Religious Sects
stories.summary: Ajay gives the history behind early American political thinking. Many of the people who settled America belonged to fringe religious sects persecuted by Europe's Catholic and Protestant establishments. These were not atheists but groups more eccentric than mainline European religion would tolerate. Separation of church and state was meant to give such sects space to practise as they liked, not to lead toward secularism, which is how the 20th century actually turned out. From this came a lasting American question: if 20 or 200 people wall themselves into a commune, which of the state's rules can they suspend, and which, like the ban on murder, must still apply? America's answer was to let people found new cities and townships with many of their own rules.
stories.insight: The secular state started as an arrangement for letting religious oddballs alone. The question of how far a community can set its own rules has been a source of energy for the American project, and Ajay thinks India would benefit from taking it seriously.
stories.quote: So there's a very deep idea in America that there should be freedom to pursue your own madness.

stories.topic: The UAE Official Who Could Pass a Law by the Day After
stories.summary: Ajay was once discussing securities law with a policymaker in the UAE. The official waved his fist and declared that if Ajay handed him the correct securities law tomorrow, he would have it enacted by the day after. He meant it as a boast about decisiveness. Ajay heard the opposite: if a law can be enacted that fast, it can be changed just as fast, so nobody has any protection.
stories.insight: Frictionless lawmaking destroys legal certainty. The slow, consultative, many-veto process of a liberal democracy is what makes a law worth something.
stories.quote: Because if a law can be enacted tomorrow, it can be reenacted the day after.

stories.summary: At the Orange City Literature Festival, an audience member asked Ajay whether he wanted India to be a tiger or an elephant. He said he wanted India to be the tortoise, chipping away for many years at sustained growth. He contrasts this with India's hare-like run of roughly 20 years of high growth from 1991 to 2011, followed by weaker years, and with the UK and the US, which grew at modest rates for a century.
stories.insight: The magic is sustained growth. Decency, consultation and fewer mistakes, kept up over decades, beat a heroic sprint.
stories.quote: What is your dream for India? Do you want to be a tiger or do you want to be an elephant? And I said, I want us to be the tortoise. That you want to chip away for long years and get sustained growth.

recommendations.item: The policy questions around airlines
recommendations.creator: Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Ajay opens the first chapter with his recent article on public policy in the airline industry.
recommendations.reason: It is a deep dive into a single industry. He uses it to raise the episode's opening question: is it better to work through one practical case at a time or to learn the general principles in their own right?

recommendations.item: Fixing the Knowledge Society (Episode 24 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit notes that the hosts discussed in a past episode how universities do a terrible job of liberal arts education. The episode is linked in the show notes.
recommendations.reason: Background for their shared view that the humanities make you a more rounded person, that universities fail to provide them, and that you have to educate yourself through books, films and art.

recommendations.item: In Service of the Republic
recommendations.creator: Vijay Kelkar and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit previews the next episode, on when the state should make policy and what public policy even means.
recommendations.reason: Amit calls it Ajay's 'masterpiece of a book'. It treats in detail the questions the follow-up episode will cover.

recommendations.item: Every Act of Government Is an Act of Violence
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit mentions writing this piece for the Times of India while making the episode's central argument.
recommendations.reason: It sets out his core claim that the existence of the state is itself violence. Every state action therefore carries a moral cost that has to be justified.

recommendations.item: Your maid funds Unani (2007)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside Amit's argument that your domestic help is a taxpayer every time she buys salt.
recommendations.reason: It takes apart the myth that only about 3% of Indians pay taxes. The cost of state spending falls on the poorest too.

recommendations.item: Taxes Should Be Used for Governance, Not Politics
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside the discussion of taxation as coercion.
recommendations.reason: It continues the episode's argument that because taxes are taken by force, how they are spent has to be justified.

recommendations.item: Where Your Taxes Go (India Uncut series)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma
recommendations.context: Amit reads examples aloud from his old blog's long-running list of wasteful state spending.
recommendations.reason: A memorable catalogue, from moustache allowances to sixty-two sandstone elephants, of what coerced money ends up paying for.

recommendations.item: Anarchy, State, and Utopia
recommendations.creator: Robert Nozick
recommendations.context: After calling the state an act of violence, Amit clarifies that he is not arguing for abolishing it. He mentions 'marvelous books' on how such questions can lead to a good equilibrium and recommends Nozick's.
recommendations.reason: He calls it a 'great book' and recommends it as the place to engage seriously with the question of anarchy versus the state.

recommendations.item: Caged Tiger: How Too Much Government Is Holding Indians Back
recommendations.creator: Subhashish Bhadra
recommendations.context: Amit cites it while comparing the American and Indian constitutions.
recommendations.reason: He calls it an excellent book. It gave him the frame that constitutions are contextual: America's was built to protect people from the state, India's to protect the state from the people.

recommendations.item: Subhashish Bhadra on Our Dysfunctional State (Episode 333 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Subhashish Bhadra
recommendations.context: Amit mentions doing an episode with Bhadra about Caged Tiger.
recommendations.reason: A longer conversation about the book's ideas on India's overreaching state.

recommendations.item: State Building
recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: Amit introduces it as the source of the scope-and-strength framework at the heart of Chapter 3.
recommendations.reason: It is a slim book, and Amit recommends everyone read it. It replaces the vague 'big state vs small state' debate with two separate dimensions: how much a state tries to do and how well it does it.

recommendations.item: Restaurant Regulations in India (Episode 18 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Madhu Menon
recommendations.context: The source of the excise-versus-fire-safety door contradiction Amit describes.
recommendations.reason: A concrete account of how an overreaching state makes honest business impossible and bribes unavoidable.

recommendations.item: Going from strong as in scary to strong as in capable
recommendations.creator: Suyash Rai and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes alongside Ajay's argument about what a 'strong state' should mean.
recommendations.reason: It sets out the distinction Ajay makes in the episode: India should want strength meaning competence, not strength meaning the power to jail anyone or pass any law overnight.

recommendations.item: The Importance of the 1991 Reforms (Episode 237 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with Shruti Rajagopalan and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit mentions having done many Seen and the Unseen episodes on the reforms while discussing 'discover, not design'.
recommendations.reason: It covers how freeing parts of the economy in 1991 set off a process of discovery and positive-sum trade that produced India's growth spurt.

recommendations.item: Why Freedom Matters (Episode 10 of Everything is Everything)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah
recommendations.context: Amit refers to the earlier episode on freedom when discussing the post-1991 period.
recommendations.reason: It makes the case that freedom drives discovery and growth, the idea this episode builds on.

recommendations.item: Essays on Nationalism
recommendations.creator: Rabindranath Tagore
recommendations.context: Ajay's recommendation for the episode. He says it is not directly on the topic, 'and yet everything is interconnected.'
recommendations.reason: He calls it one of the most beautiful books in the world and Tagore one of the most beautiful writers of the English language. The ideas are deep, powerful and timeless, and the book is slim enough that a lazy reader has no excuse.

recommendations.item: The Libertarian Reader
recommendations.creator: David Boaz
recommendations.context: Amit's recommendation, introduced after he reads out a Boaz quote about the state.
recommendations.reason: It collects essays by liberal thinkers such as Milton Friedman and Friedrich Hayek, a good distillation of many strands of thought. Amit asks readers not to be put off by the label in the title.

recommendations.item: What is Libertarianism? (Episode 117 of The Seen and the Unseen)
recommendations.creator: Amit Varma with David Boaz
recommendations.context: Amit mentions that Boaz has been on his show and says the episode will be linked.
recommendations.reason: A chance to hear Boaz discuss the ideas behind the book in conversation.

recommendations.item: The Origins of Political Order
recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: The first of a two-part work Amit recommends after State Building.
recommendations.reason: He calls the two volumes magisterial. Over a long sweep of history they show how the state evolved, which you need in order to understand the interplay between state and society.

recommendations.item: Political Order and Political Decay
recommendations.creator: Francis Fukuyama
recommendations.context: The second volume of the same work.
recommendations.reason: It completes Fukuyama's history of the state's evolution and helps you see the state-society relationship more clearly.

recommendations.item: Kashi Ka Assi
recommendations.creator: Kashinath Singh
recommendations.context: Linked in the show notes where Amit quotes, in a 'family-friendly version', the line 'Bharme jaaye duniya, hum bajaayein harmonia'.
recommendations.reason: The line sums up the temptation to tune out a world going to hell. Amit uses it to argue the opposite: if you care about the world, you have to understand it.

recommendations.item: Pune Public Policy Festival (January 19-20, 2024)
recommendations.context: The episode's sponsor. This year's theme is 'Tradeoffs'.
recommendations.reason: Pune, once called the 'Oxford of the East', may be pulling some of the policy conversation away from Delhi. The festival brings young professionals together with policy experts, bureaucrats, economists and thinkers to debate tradeoffs such as environment vs growth, growth vs equality, and technology vs privacy.

core_ideas.explanation: You can learn the mechanics of a field or keep asking why. Amit's poker players memorised ranges without understanding them. Ajay's example is engineering: a technician trained on one air conditioner can repair it, but without thermodynamics and advanced physics they cannot invent the next one or follow developments like solid-state heat pumps. Ajay thinks India over-values job-ready vocational training. A liberal arts education is in one sense useless, but its general principles prepare a 20-year-old for a world that will keep changing over their working life.
core_ideas.quote: in some ways the most useless thing in the world is the liberal arts education. You're absolutely not job ready. But you know what? It's the best kind of education because those general principles prepare you for that seventy, eighty years of working life which stands in front of a twenty year old today.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's view on explaining ideas. A story grabs attention, but the principle it teaches often floats free and gets forgotten. A framework of first principles and root causes can be applied to anything, and its flaws are out in the open where people can argue with them. Hence his love of economics, which he sees as the study of human behaviour: scarcity and incentives show up in policy, literature, art and music.
core_ideas.quote: often that principle is sort of adrift in space, you know, by itself and easily forgotten. It's like a fancy lesson in LinkedIn.

core_ideas.explanation: Liberalism says everyone has rights that no one should infringe. But rights only mean something if they are defended, and defending them requires a state with a monopoly on violence. So we have to give up some of our rights to protect the rest.
core_ideas.quote: liberalism says that we all have rights and no one should infringe them. And yet for those rights to have meaning and to be protected, we have to give away some of the rights.

core_ideas.concept: Every Act of Government Is an Act of Violence
core_ideas.explanation: Amit's claim is that the state itself is violence, not just some of what it does. It is funded by taxes that nobody would pay unless forced, under threat of imprisonment, much like a monopoly mafia. That doesn't make the state illegitimate, since we need it. But every ideology, whether communist, libertarian or social democrat, has to answer one central question: for what purposes is this violence justified, and why?
core_ideas.quote: whatever the state does, it does through violence. And therefore you have to justify that

core_ideas.explanation: Add up direct and indirect taxes and perhaps a third of your income goes to the state. That means you spend roughly January to April each year working for the state rather than for yourself. Amit offers this as a way to see the real cost of the state: we are not completely free.
core_ideas.quote: If one third of your income goes in taxes, that means that between January and April every year, you don't work for yourself, you work for the state. That means we are all essentially in part time slavery.

core_ideas.explanation: The claim that only about 3% of Indians pay taxes confuses income tax with all taxes. The domestic help buying salt and the beggar buying tea or milk for a baby both pay indirect taxes. Inflation, caused by the government expanding the money supply, works as a tax on the poor. So every state expense, from a space programme to a statue, is partly paid for by the poorest people.
core_ideas.quote: You know, your domestic help, when she buys salt, she's a taxpayer.

core_ideas.concept: Normalised Taxation: The Dandi March Benchmark
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay points out that the British tax levels that provoked Gandhi's Dandi March were modest compared with the taxes independent India levies. What once set off a mass movement is now accepted without much thought.
core_ideas.quote: The levels of taxation imposed by the British that kicked off Gandhiji's Dandi March are actually modest and decent compared to the levels of taxation in independent India.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's distinction: the state's monopoly on violence works through two channels. One is taxation, which raises money to spend. That channel has a natural check: raising revenue is hard, rupees are fungible, people hate paying, and budgets force some discipline. The other channel is direct coercion, rules saying 'thou shalt not' backed by punishment. Nobody keeps a single ledger of these, so hundreds of agencies add new restrictions every year unchecked. Ajay thinks this may be the bigger problem for public administration.
core_ideas.quote: There is no single statement that details and documents all the acts of state coercion. And year after year, the state just layers on more and more and more coercion and nobody keeps track of it.

core_ideas.explanation: From Subhashish Bhadra's Caged Tiger. America's constitution came out of people fleeing persecution, so it protects the people from the state. India's was written amid Partition's violence, when it was unclear whether the centre would hold, so it centralised power and protects the state from the people. Amit argues this inversion still shapes a mindset in which citizens exist to serve the state and the state's reach keeps growing.
core_ideas.quote: not protecting the people from the state, but the state from the people.

core_ideas.explanation: Fukuyama's framework replaces the vague 'big state vs small state' debate with two dimensions. Scope is how many things the state tries to do, from defence and law and order up to roads, temples, pilgrimage subsidies and space programmes. Strength is state capacity, how well it does those things. Sierra Leone is low on both, close to anarchy. The USSR had huge scope and middling strength. Amit's ideal is limited scope with great strength. India is the reverse: it meddles in bedrooms and businesses, and Amit has read that setting up a business in Delhi takes more licences than getting a gun. Meanwhile it fails at its core jobs. In Amit's view there is effectively no rule of law in India except for the privileged.
core_ideas.quote: the ideal state, what I believe, is a state where the scope is limited and the strength is massive.

core_ideas.concept: Strong as Capable, Not Strong as Scary
core_ideas.explanation: Ajay criticises two ideas of 'strong' popular with India's middle class. One is a state that can grab the most powerful people and put them in jail. The other is a leader who can announce a new law or policy overnight. He rejects both. A strong state should mean a competent one: handling COVID vaccination policy so that as few people as possible die in a second wave, or reaching every child with a polio vaccine within a year or two.
core_ideas.quote: When we say strong state, we should focus the word strong as in competence.

core_ideas.concept: Slowness Is a Feature, Not a Bug
core_ideas.explanation: Liberal democracy disperses power: no single decision-maker, checks and balances, many people able to veto. That makes it look slow and shambolic, and that is the point. Amit adds that the rules should be designed so the system is robust: even the worst strongman you can imagine should be able to do only limited damage. Ajay sees the admiration for strongmen as a symptom of India's failure to teach the humanities.
core_ideas.quote: that makes it appear slow and shambolic, and that's a feature, not a bug.

core_ideas.explanation: Amit's heroes of the freedom struggle are the 19th-century classical liberals: Dadabhai Naoroji, Gopal Ganesh Agarkar, Ranade and Gopal Krishna Gokhale. They wanted a freer, more just society but pursued it through engagement, discourse and dialogue rather than overnight revolution. Hoping for someone to seize power and impose liberalism is not liberal, because whoever can impose it can just as easily impose its opposite.
core_ideas.quote: If today somebody can come and impose liberalism, tomorrow somebody can come and lock you up and send you into gulags.

core_ideas.explanation: India's per capita GDP in PPP terms is about one-ninth of America's, which is a little over three doublings. At 7% real per capita growth, income doubles every 10 years, so 30 years would bring India within reach of today's United States. But Ajay notes that 7% per capita growth sustained for 30 years has essentially never happened in world history. Forcing it through dictatorship brings short-lived, Hitler- or Stalin-style mobilisation and then disaster. Ajay calls catching up in 30 years the wrong goal.
core_ideas.quote: That's a bad dream, that's a wrong objective to pursue. And I think that the people who chase those kinds of objectives haven't thought deeply about the process of economic development.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay's phrase, which Amit links to Adam Ferguson's observation that much social progress comes from human action but not human design. The growth after 1991 came from freeing parts of the economy so people could discover positive-sum trades, not from government programmes aiming at 7% or 8%. India didn't free up enough, and growth targets imposed from above are bound to backfire.
core_ideas.quote: we organically discover, not design, what it means to be a healthy liberal society.

core_ideas.explanation: Ajay distinguishes two motives for learning. One is instrumental: if you want to work in business or government, you need to understand the world. The other is amusement: even if you have shut yourself off behind high walls, you'll enjoy the spectacle more if you understand it, the way a chess game is more fun to watch the more chess you know.
core_ideas.quote: If you know more about chess, you'll actually have a more interesting ride as you watch this.

jokes_and_cultural_references.content: Amit, after Ajay's crash into a spotless glass wall: 'in terms of clarity, there is something that is out there that can match the clarity of your prose. So, you know, compliment to both you and the glass wall.'

Ajay to a commenter who said he was too lazy to work things out himself: 'So you, gentle reader, how dare you be lazy? Your immortal soul deserves better. Get off your butt and start by reading a slim book.'
Amit, when Ajay recommends Tagore: 'my heart fills with joy that you named my fellow Bengali Robida, and I almost feel like you're flirting with me.'

Amit finally understands Ajay's 'thirty-year sprint': tortoises live for centuries, so for them 30 years really is a sprint. The tortoise, he imagines, listens to Hindustani classical. Ajay adds The Seen and the Unseen, and Amit runs with it: 'which is often heard by hares at double speed, which is also perfectly fine. We cater to hares, we cater to tortoises, and we cater to some human beings.'

David Boaz, read out by Amit: 'Conservatives want to be your dad, telling you what to do and what not to do. Liberals want to be your mommy, feeding you, tucking you in and wiping your nose. Libertarians want to treat you as an adult.' Amit clarifies that Boaz means American welfare-state liberals, and urges listeners to drop labels and think about principles.
Ajay interjects with a line he attributes to Churchill: 'Dogs look up to us. Cats look down on us. Pigs treat us as equals.' Amit: 'Beautifully said.'
Adam Ferguson's idea of social progress as the result of 'human action, but not human design', which Amit uses to back Ajay's 'discover, not design'.

Amit's 'family-friendly version' of a Banarasi line: 'Bharme jaaye duniya, hum bajaayein harmonia' (let the world go to hell, I'll play my harmonium). He admits he is sometimes in 'harmonia mode'. The show notes link Kashinath Singh's Kashi Ka Assi.
Pune as 'the Oxford of the East', an intellectual hub of India whose influence shifted to Delhi after Independence. Amit raises it in the sponsor message for the Pune Public Policy Festival.

Ajay's sign-off: 'Did you ever think that there would be an episode of Everything Is Everything in which seven different animals would be mentioned? We've had a cat, a dog, a pig, a tiger, elephant, tortoise, and a hare.'
Amit's closing line: 'We are all turtles on the march of knowledge towards the end of history.'
